q: They’re not interrupting or being rude. Nor are they breaking any rules. But it gets on your last nerve.
The best response, however, isn’t to shoo them away or tell them to mind their own business. No, the best response is to give them exactly what they want.
Although it may go against your every impulse, lean in and hear them out. Place your hand on your chin, look them in the eye, and take their concerns seriously.
If you embrace the concerns students bring to you, and validate them with your response, it tends to happen less often, not more.
It’s also their way of making a connection with you. It’s a moment you share together, pulling in the same direction.
So don’t mess it up. Don’t send them away, cut them off in annoyance, or risk sullying your relationship. Instead, welcome their thoughts. It takes just a few extra seconds of your time.

t: How To Handle A Student Who Rejects Your Kindness
q: They meet your smile, your generosity, and your kindness with indifference—and even cruelty.
You daydream about putting them in their place. You lay awake rehearsing a lecture they won’t soon forget.
Maybe they’ve been burned so many times and so deeply that if they allow themselves to like you—or worse, look up to you—and you let them down, the blow would be too great.
Maybe they’ve erected a hard shell over shattered trust and the possibility of disappointment and betrayal.
You give your patience and your understanding. You give your steadiness and your consistency. You give your unrelenting, unbending, undefeatable kindness.
Maybe this will be the day they accept you and let you in. Maybe it will be in a week or a month or on the last day of school.
x: Names the genuine hurt and anger teachers feel when sustained kindness toward a student is met with indifference or cruelty.

q: That doesn’t mean that it doesn’t hurt when you’re ignored or your good work goes unnoticed.
According to research, recognition is one of the biggest keys to job satisfaction. When an employee feels valued and appreciated, they’re more motivated and confident in their abilities.
Few principals are experts in classroom management. Fewer still were experts when they were in the classroom.

As a new teacher, low in confidence, one former boss used to leave cards and notes in my mailbox assuring me I was doing well. She would point out specifically what she liked, guiding me down the right and effective path.
They were people, first and foremost, and knew that they were the chief engine that drove positive school culture, morale, and pride in being a Ram or Eagle or Viking.
It isn’t about you and your shortcomings. It’s about them and theirs.

t: How To Handle Students Who Complain
q: It can take willpower not to reply with a sharp, “Because I said so” or “So sad, too bad.” It can be hard not to glare, fume, and hold a private grudge.
It helps to remember that they’re just kids, and complaining is part of growing up. It’s in their DNA, and okay.
Sometimes a genuine smile is all you need. But if they persist, tell them that you understand—because you do.

Students get irritated when they don’t know why you’re doing what you’re doing. So tell them. Be transparent. Studies show that when you use the word ‘because’ you’ll experience greater influence and buy-in, even if the reason is nonsensical.
The key to getting them through those tough moments is your empathy and unwillingness to take their complaining personally.
They set aside their compulsion to complain and avoid difficulty, and instead embrace it as part of the pursuit of excellence you live and breathe and pursue every day.
